verses.text: Benjamin became the father of Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,
Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.
Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud,
Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,
Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.
These are the sons of Ehud. These are the heads of fathers’ households of the inhabitants of Geba, who were carried captive to Manahath:
Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, who carried them captive; and he became the father of Uzza and Ahihud.
Shaharaim became the father of children in the field of Moab, after he had sent them away. Hushim and Baara were his wives.
By Hodesh his wife, he became the father of Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam,
Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers’ households.
By Hushim, he became the father of Abitub and Elpaal.
The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod, with its towns;
and Beriah, and Shema, who were heads of fathers’ households of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who put to flight the inhabitants of Gath;
and Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth,
Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,
Michael, Ishpah, Joha, the sons of Beriah,
Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,
Ishmerai, Izliah, Jobab, the sons of Elpaal,
Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi,
Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,
Adaiah, Beraiah, Shimrath, the sons of Shimei,
Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,
Abdon, Zichri, Hanan,
Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,
Iphdeiah, Penuel, the sons of Shashak,
Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah,
Jaareshiah, Elijah, Zichri, and the sons of Jeroham.
These were heads of fathers’ households throughout their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.
The father of Gibeon, whose wife’s name was Maacah, lived in Gibeon,
with his firstborn son Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,
Gedor, Ahio, and Zecher.
Mikloth became the father of Shimeah. They also lived with their brothers in Jerusalem, near their brothers.
Ner became the father of Kish. Kish became the father of Saul. Saul became the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
The son of Jonathan was Merib Baal. Merib Baal became the father of Micah.
The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.
Ahaz became the father of Jehoaddah. Jehoaddah became the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri became the father of Moza.
Moza became the father of Binea. Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, and Azel his son.
Azel had six sons, whose names are these: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.
The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third.
The sons of Ulam were mighty men of valor, archers, and had many sons, and sons’ sons, one hundred fifty. All these were of the sons of Benjamin.

footnotes.content: Benjamin's sons begin a whole lineage of the faithful remnant. Notice the order—each name a thread held tight by the God who promised never to leave His people without a voice. These are the ones who would anchor Judah's return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nohah and Rapha complete Benjamin's immediate sons—the fourth and fifth branches. I see in genealogies like this that God counts every name, every generation. None are forgotten, even when the world thought the line was broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bela's children—Addar, Gera, Abihud—extend the family further. Each generation builds on the faithfulness of the last, a living chain of covenant people. The Lord was weaving His purpose through Benjamin long before the exile, and never let the thread snap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah—more descendants, more proof that God's people multiply and spread. Even in a list of names, I sense the quiet miracle: God preserved His people when it looked like all would be lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram close Bela's line. I've always loved how the Chronicler keeps naming—it's a song of remembrance, a way of saying, 'You matter to God, and we won't let you disappear from the story.' Exile could scatter people, but not memory in God's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ehud's sons became heads of families in Geba and were carried captive to Manahath—a hard naming of deportation, yet the record survives. Even exile is held in God's memory, and those scattered are never erased from His book.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera led the captivity—and yet they became fathers themselves, Uzza and Ahihud following after. What strikes me is that captors and captives both live on in God's plan, and both are named. Nothing is wasted in His sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shaharaim sent away his wives Hushim and Baara, then fathered children in the field of Moab—a life fractured and strange, yet still held in the genealogy. I see in this hard honesty that God's record doesn't hide broken families; it keeps them whole in His memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By Hodesh, Shaharaim fathered Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam—a new beginning, a new wife, more sons. Life moved on even in exile, even in loss. God's mercy flows through our worst seasons, giving new names and new chances to those who belong to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeuz, Shachia, Mirmah—Shaharaim's sons who became heads of households. Even in displacement, leadership remained, and families held their shape. I see the Lord's hand keeping His people organized and purposeful, no matter the storm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushim's children were Abitub and Elpaal—another wife, another line carried forward. The genealogy doesn't hide the complexity of a life split across wives and exile, but includes it. God's love meets us where we actually are, however tangled the path.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elpaal's sons Eber and Misham—and Shemed who built Ono and Lod. Here builders emerge from exile, people who took rubble and made towns again. I see in this that God grants His people not only survival but the grace to rebuild what was lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beriah and Shema were heads of fathers' households in Aijalon, and they put to flight the inhabitants of Gath—a rare glimpse of military prowess, a reminder that even after exile, God's people could stand and resist. Weakness is never the Lord's final word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth—more sons, more branches spreading. I notice the genealogy keeps listing without apology or summary; each name is a thread, and the whole pattern is what matters. God doesn't compress His people down; He preserves their multitude.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebadiah, Arad, Eder—three more, each real to the Lord, each counted. I've learned that God's arithmetic isn't about grand totals; it's about knowing each face, each name. These lists remind me that I'm never one of millions to Him—I'm known by name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michael, Ishpah, Joha—Beriah's descendants continuing the line. The Lord weaves families through generations like a craftsman with thread, each color distinct yet part of one whole. Beriah's branch reached deep into Benjamin's restored settlement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber—Elpaal's line carries forward, each name a link to the covenant. What strikes me is that these genealogies span captivity and return; they're proof that exile didn't end the story—God's purpose ran right through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmerai, Izliah, Jobab—more of Elpaal's sons, building the family tree through remembered names. I've come to treasure how these lists honor each person, not as a footnote but as someone whose life mattered to God's plan.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi—another cluster of names, another household. The Lord built His people back not as one mass but as families, each with its own story and place. That's how grace works—restoring us not in theory but in real relationships.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel—yet more children, yet more proof that the remnant was alive and fruitful. I see the Lord's blessing in every name, in the sheer fact that Benjamin didn't disappear but flourished, bearing children even after exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adaiah, Beraiah, Shimrath—Shimei's sons, another branch of the family taking shape. I notice the genealogy doesn't rush through these names; each is given time to exist, to be known. That's how God treats His people: with unhurried, personal attention.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel—more sons of Shimei, extending the line. I've noticed that in these genealogies, the Lord preserves not just the famous but the faithful faithful, the ones who quietly held the faith through exile and built again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abdon, Zichri, Hanan—three more names in a long chain. What I treasure here is that God's commitment to His people wasn't conditional on their wealth or fame; it was absolute, written in genealogies that survive empires.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah—still more sons, still more families. I see in the length of these lists that God delights in abundance, in the fruitfulness of His people even when the world called them defeated. Our God is a God of multiplication.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Iphdeiah, Penuel—Shashak's descendants, another branch rooting itself back into the promised land. I'm moved by how the genealogy keeps building, name after name, as if to say, 'See? The Lord never abandoned His people. Here they are, alive and remembered.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah—more of Shashak's line, keeping the family rooted. There's something deeply comforting about being included in a genealogy, about knowing your name will outlast kingdoms. That's what the Lord offers His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jaareshiah, Elijah, Zichri—and Jeroham's sons as well. I notice these weren't the kings or prophets we'd expect to hear; they were ordinary faithful who held the line and kept covenant. The Lord honors obscurity that trusts Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These chiefs lived in Jerusalem—the moment the genealogy surfaces from names into place. After exile, Benjamin's leaders returned and took their place in the holy city again, heads of households, restoring community. God's promise to gather His people came true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The father of Gibeon lived there with his wife Maacah—now we move to a specific household in a specific place. Gibeon wasn't the center of power, but it mattered, and the genealogy marks it. The Lord cares about every settlement, every family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abdon his firstborn, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab—five sons built this household. I see in Kish's name a connection forward (he would father Saul), but here he's simply one of five, one part of a beloved family. The Lord lifts up the humble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gedor, Ahio, Zecher—three more sons, completing the count of Gibeon's house. I notice the genealogy keeps the family intact, naming them all, making clear that each child was known and loved. God builds His kingdom through real families, not abstractions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mikloth became the father of Shimeah, and they lived near their brothers in Jerusalem—family staying close, bonds held tight. I've learned that one of God's deepest gifts is kinship, the chance to live near those who share your faith and story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ner became the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan—here the genealogy names the first king of Israel, and his son, Jonathan, whose loyalty to God ran deeper than to dynasty. One moment the line is obscure Benjamites, the next it touches royalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan's son was Merib Baal, and Merib Baal fathered Micah—the royal line continues through the exile, though now hidden, no longer on a throne. Even displaced, God's people carry purpose; even in loss, there's a hidden kingship that belongs to Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micah's sons—Pithon, Melech, Tarea, Ahaz—the line extends into obscurity, names that belong now to descendants unnamed in the narrative. This is where genealogies lead: to people who served the Lord in complete silence, known only to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, who fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri—and Zimri fathered Moza. I see how deeply the genealogy runs, tracing bloodlines through generations of exile and return. Not one name was forgotten in God's reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moza fathered Binea, Raphah, Eleasah, Azel—the line continues deeper still, each generation a link to the promise. I'm struck by the Lord's faithfulness: even when His people seemed forgotten, He held the thread of their covenant steady.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azel had six sons—Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, Hanan—a full household, a branch bearing fruit. Even at the end of the genealogy's deep reach, we see God's blessing: families, names, purpose, all held in His hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eshek's brother had sons—Ulam the firstborn, Jeush, Eliphelet—another household, another testament to God's covenant enduring. These names will never be famous, yet here they are, written forever in Israel's genealogy, in the record of God's faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ulam's sons were mighty men of valor, archers with many descendants—one hundred fifty. Readers today hear an echo: strength doesn't come from prominence but from trust in the God who names us and holds us. Benjamin's lineage carried the sacred trust through exile to restoration, and we still bear witness to that faithfulness. As of 2026-10, I see in this the Lord's promise: my name, too, is written in a genealogy that will outlast empires.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
